common_name: Bradford Pear (Original Thornless Ornamental Callery Pear)

planting.note: WARNING: This was the first Callery pear cultivar sold for ornamental use and is now discouraged or restricted in many areas because of storm damage and invasive seed set; confirm local rules before planting.

directions: 'Bradford' was the original ornamental selection of Callery pear, chosen at a USDA research station in the mid-twentieth century for a dense, symmetrical oval crown, an absence of thorns, and a heavy cover of white flowers that opens before the leaves each spring. Glossy foliage turns strong shades of red, orange, and purple in fall, but the tight, narrow angles where its branches meet the trunk make mature trees notoriously prone to splitting apart in wind, ice, or heavy snow after fifteen to twenty years. Although bred to be largely self-sterile, it readily cross-pollinates with other Callery pear cultivars growing nearby, producing abundant fertile seed that birds have spread into wild areas across the eastern and midwestern United States, so its sale and planting are now banned or restricted in a growing number of states. Where it can still legally be planted, give it full sun and well-drained soil and plan for a showy but relatively short ornamental life before storm damage or removal becomes likely.

common_name: Cleveland Select Callery Pear (Chanticleer Columnar Flowering Pear)

planting.note: WARNING: Like all named Callery pear cultivars its sale and planting are now limited or banned in a growing number of states; confirm local rules before planting.

directions: Cleveland Select is a narrow, columnar Callery pear sold under this trade name but identical to the clone marketed elsewhere as 'Chanticleer,' both propagated from a single chance seedling found in Ohio decades ago. Its tight, uniform branch angles hold together far better in wind, ice, and snow than the older 'Bradford' cultivar, which is why it largely replaced 'Bradford' in street tree and specimen plantings from the 1980s onward. Clusters of white flowers open on bare branches ahead of the foliage each spring, and the narrow, glossy leaves color up in yellow, orange, and red before dropping in fall. As with every named Callery pear cultivar, it cross-pollinates freely with other selections growing nearby and sets abundant viable seed that birds carry into wild areas, so like 'Bradford,' its sale and planting are now limited or banned in a growing number of states.
